Chapter 10 — Contemporary Orthodontic Appliances

Plain text is your original summary, kept word-for-word. Coloured boxes are genuine 7th-edition additions (green = new, amber = changed/reversed); red marks important cautions. Figures sit in the right margin (zoom to read the book caption).
Removable Appliances
  • Modern removable appliance therapy consists largely of the use of:
    1. Active aligners with springs for tooth movement, used primarily in preadolescents
    2. Various types of functional appliances for growth guidance
    3. Clear plastic aligners for tooth movement in adults.

I Development of Active Aligners

  • In the early 1900s, George Crozat developed a removable appliance fabricated entirely of precious metal Fig 10.1.
  • Martin Schwarz developed and publicized a variety of "split plate" appliances, which were effective for expanding the dental arches Fig 10.2.
  • Philip Adams modified the arrowhead clasp favored by Schwarz into the Adams crib Fig 10.3, which is still the most effective clasp for removable appliances
  • Tooth movement with removable appliances in children almost always falls into one of two major categories:
    • Arch expansion, with jackscrew as an active element
    • Repositioning of individual teeth, used only when a few millimeters of tipping movement are acceptable.

II Functional Appliances for Growth Modification

  • By definition, a functional appliance is one that changes the posture of the mandible, holding it open or open and forward. Table 10.1
  • The monobloc in the early 1900s is generally considered the forerunner of all functional appliances, but the activator in the 1920s Fig 10.4 was the first to be widely accepted.
  • Functional appliances falls into one of four broad categories:
    • Passive tooth-borne
      • Depend only on soft tissue stretch and muscular activity to produce effects.
      • Examples: the Bionator "always removable" Fig 10.5, twin block "usually removable, can be fixed" Fig 10.6, and Herbst appliance "usually fixed, can be removable" Fig 10.7A.
    • Forsus Appliance (it produce greater skeletal effect on maxilla, more dental and less skeletal effect on mandible, compared to Herbst)
    • Active tooth-borne (Include expansion screws or springs to move teeth)
    • Tissue-borne (The Frankel appliance is the only tissue-borne functional appliance) Fig 10.8
    • Hybrid (used primarily in the treatment of jaw asymmetry) Fig 10.9
New in 7th ed — Carriere Motion appliance A newer Class II corrector: it places a distal force on the maxillary posterior teeth while pushing the mandible forward (via Class II elastics) to correct the molar relationship first, after which a fixed appliance or aligners finish the case. A claimed advantage is minimal restriction of lateral mandibular excursions. As with other advertised Class II devices, robust skeletal/dental evidence beyond case reports is still limited.

III Clear Aligner Therapy

Current Considerations in Clinical Use of Clear Aligners

  • It is clear now that clear aligners can perform well for many but not all malocclusions (Box 10.1)
  • The use of attachments bonded to selected teeth greatly extends the possible tooth movement with aligners, but even with attachments, significant torque and correction of molar relationships is difficult.
  • A refinement or midcourse correction often is necessary when tracking deviates significantly from the plan.
  • Can be used to bleach during treatment (unless patient has bonded attachments)
New in 7th ed Some 3D-printing resins are now commercially available that allow the direct printing of aligners — without the need for model fabrication and thermoforming — although the material properties are still being refined.
Fixed Appliances

I The Development of Contemporary Fixed Appliances

Angle's Progression to the Edgewise Appliance

  • Angle developed four major appliance systems:
    • E-arch, Angle's first appliance, capable only of tipping teeth to a new position Fig 10.16
    • Pin and tube, used a vertical tube on each tooth into which a soldered pin from a smaller archwire was placed (trying to achieve more than tipping movement).
    • Ribbon arch
      • Modified the tube on each tooth to provide a vertically positioned rectangular slot behind the tube. A ribbon archwire of 10 × 20 gold wire was placed into the vertical slot and held with pins Fig 10.17.
      • The major weakness of the appliance was that it provided relatively poor control of root position.
    • Edgewise (90-degree angle to the plane of insertion of the ribbon arch)
      • Angle reoriented the slot from vertical to horizontal.
      • The dimensions of the slot were altered to 22 × 28 mil, and a 22 × 28 precious metal wire was used.

Other Early Fixed Appliance Systems — Labiolingual, Twin Wire

  • The labiolingual appliance used bands on first molars and a combination of heavy lingual and labial archwires to which fingersprings were soldered to move individual teeth.
  • The twin-wire appliance used bands on incisors as well as molars and featured twin 10-mil steel archwires for alignment of the incisor teeth.
  • Neither of these appliances was capable of more than tipping movements. They have disappeared from contemporary use.

Begg Appliance

  • Raymond Begg had been taught use of the ribbon arch appliance at the Angle school. He also concluded that extraction of teeth was often necessary, and set out to adapt the ribbon arch appliance so that it could be used for better control of root position Fig 10.19.
  • Begg's adaptation took three forms:
    1. He replaced the precious metal ribbon arch with high-strength 16-mil round stainless steel wire.
    2. He retained the original ribbon arch bracket, but turned it upside down so that the bracket slot pointed gingivally rather than occlusally
    3. He added auxiliary springs to the appliance for control of root position.
  • "Binding" was minimized because Begg's strategy for anchorage control was tipping and uprighting.
  • The Begg appliance is rarely seen now in contemporary use; it still appears now in the hybrid Tip-Edge appliance, with brackets that allow the use of rectangular wires in finishing Fig 10.20.

Contemporary Edgewise

  • Major steps in the evolution of the edgewise appliance include:
    • Automatic rotational control
    • Alteration in bracket slot dimensions (to 18-mil)
    • Straight-wire bracket prescriptions "the key step in improving the efficiency of the edgewise appliance"
New in 7th ed The long-discussed 20-slot appliance (a compromise between 18- and 22-slot) has, only recently, begun to be implemented by some of the digitally assisted bracket systems.

II Bands for Attachments

Indications for Banding

  • Heavy intermittent forces against the attachments "the primary indication for banding". An example is an upper first molar against extraoral force.
  • Teeth that will need both labial and lingual attachments. Isolated bonded lingual attachments that are not tied to some other part of the appliance can be swallowed or aspirated if something comes loose.
  • Teeth with short clinical crowns; the band displace the gingiva as it is carried into proper position, and the decision to band rather than bond second premolars in adolescents is often based on the length of the clinical crown.

Steps in Banding

  • Separation: Two main methods of separation are used for posterior teeth:
    1. Separating springs, opening enough space for banding in approximately 1 week Fig 10.22
    2. Elastomeric separators ("doughnuts"), squeeze the teeth apart over a period of several days (They exert heavy force initially that declines quickly, usually painful)
  • Fitting bands:
    • Maxillary molar band is designed to be placed initially by hand pressure on an instrument placed on proximal surfaces. Then it is driven to place by biting pressure on the mesiobuccal and distolingual surfaces. The final seating is with heavy biting force on the distolingual corner.
    • Lower molar bands are designed to be seated initially with hand pressure on the proximal surfaces and then with heavy biting force along the buccal but not the lingual margins.
  • Cementation: New cements specifically designed for orthodontic use have supplanted the zinc phosphate and early glass ionomer cements, are a composite of glass ionomer and resin materials.

III Bonded Attachments

(Direct / Indirect bonding)

  • Trials with modified glass ionomers for bonding showed that even when some composite resin was included in the bonding material, the bond strength still was not adequate.
  • The key to bonding with a largely glass ionomer material has turned out to be deproteinization of the enamel surface with 5% NaOCl (sodium hypochlorite, widely sold as Clorox), and then a 15- to 20-second etch time—slightly shorter than the usual 25 to 30 seconds—with 35% H₃PO₄. This increases the percentage of etch patterns 1 and 2 in the enamel surface Fig 10.27, and significantly increases the bond strength of the resin-modified glass ionomer (Fuji Ortho LC).
  • A light nickel–titanium (NiTi) wire without initial full bracket engagement in severely malpositioned teeth should be used because the glass ionomer part of the adhesive takes 24 hours to set.
  • With that approach, the debonding rate is said to be about 5%, roughly comparable to rates with composite resin bonding materials.

IV Characteristics of Contemporary Fixed Appliances

Appliance Materials — Stainless Steel

  • Slot dimensions are accurate to at least ±1 mil (0.025 mm)
  • Three contemporary ways to produce edgewise brackets and tubes: by metal-injection molding (MIM), casting, or 3-D printing
  • Most of the brackets and tubes for contemporary appliances still are produced by MIM.

Titanium as an Alternative to Stainless Steel

  • A major indication for titanium brackets and wires is to eliminate the possibility of an allergic response to the 8% nickel content in stainless steel.
  • The major advantage is better bond reliability. Titanium has the same strength as stainless steel, but is half as stiff. This means that a titanium bracket can absorb 50% more impact energy than a steel bracket, reducing the load on the bond during function Fig 10.29.
  • Titanium has a chemically active surface, and this can contribute to difficulty in sliding, especially with a TMA wire in a titanium bracket.

Nonmetallic Materials: Plastics, Ceramics, Composites

  • Plastic brackets have four largely unresolved problems:
    • Staining and discoloration
    • Poor strength Fig 10.29
    • Poor dimensional stability (not possible to provide precise bracket slots)
    • Friction and binding (between the plastic bracket and metal archwire make it very difficult to slide)
  • Ceramic brackets
    • Dimensionally stable
    • Apparent problems are fractures, friction within bracket slots, wear on teeth contacting a bracket, and enamel damage from bracket removal.
    • Ceramic brackets tend to be brittle. Because the fracture toughness of steel is much greater, ceramic brackets must be bulkier than stainless steel brackets.
    • Contact of an opposing tooth can abrade enamel quite rapidly.
  • Composite plastic brackets are likely to become the next advance in brackets. (better physical properties than any metal already exist and could be used for both brackets and archwires)

Straight-Wire Concept in Bracket and Tube Design

  • Compensations for First-Order Bends (offset).
    • The tube or bracket specified for the upper molar should have at least a 10-degree offset, as should the tube for the upper second molar.
    • The offset for the lower first molar should be 5 to 7 degrees. The offset for the lower second molar should be at least as large as for the first molar.
  • Compensations for Second-Order Bends (inclination) Fig 10.35
  • Compensations for Third-Order Bends (torque). Four factors are particularly germane to how much torque is used for any particular bracket:
    1. The value that the developer of the appliance chose as the average normal inclination of the tooth surface.
    2. Where on the labial surface the bracket is intended to be placed, so an appliance meant to be placed more gingivally would require different torque values than would one placed more incisally.
    3. The expected "play" between the wire and the bracket slot, which is determined by the difference between the wire size and the slot size.
    4. The resistance to unwanted movements, such as negative torque prescribed for lower incisors to resist the expected proclination from non-extraction alignment.

Contemporary Straight-Wire Brackets and Tubes

  • Self-Ligating Brackets (active or passive). A definitive review of claims versus evidence concluded that self-ligating brackets save a little time in ligation but do not produce a saving of treatment time or better results. The self-ligating brackets perform as well as conventional ones, with no evidence that their latching mechanism makes any positive or negative difference in the outcome of treatment.
  • Individually Customized Brackets. Custom brackets for facial surface of teeth offer the prospect of eliminating almost all archwire bending. The Insignia system now marketed by Ormco is the only commercial product at present. It did result in a significant decrease in both treatment time and the number of archwire changes compared with directly or indirectly bonded conventional brackets, but more of the decrease was attributed to indirect bonding than the custom brackets.
  • Lingual Appliances. Wire bending is eliminated by using wire-bending robots to form the archwires.
New in 7th ed — custom & digital bracket systems Beyond Insignia, the 7th edition adds newer fully-/semi-customized systems:
  • LightForce — a fully-customized, 3D-printed ceramic bracket system, each bracket individually designed for the tooth.
  • KL Owen — a semi-customized labial system (designed around a 19×25-mil wire in a 19.5-mil slot).
  • InBrace — a lingual system that moves teeth with a programmed, non-sliding looped archwire that snaps into modified lingual brackets (loops compensate for the short interbracket span).

Arch Form & Archwire Fabrication

  • Selection of Arch Form — Preformed arch wires:
    • When NiTi and beta-titanium wires are needed, there is no choice but to use preformed archwires because these wires are almost impossible to shape to arch form without special tools.
    • The basic principle of arch form in orthodontic treatment is that patient's original arch form should be preserved. (this would place the teeth in a position of maximum stability)
    • As a general guideline, if the maxillary and mandibular arch forms are incompatible at the beginning of treatment, the mandibular arch form should be used as a basic guide.
    • An excellent mathematical description of the natural dental arch form is provided by a catenary curve. For all patients, the fit is not as good if the catenary curve is extended posteriorly from the first molars, because the dental arch normally curves slightly lingually in the second and third molar region Fig 10.43A.
    • Another mathematical model, originally advocated by Brader and often called the Brader arch form, is based on a trifocal ellipse Fig 10.43B. The Brader arch form therefore will more closely approximate the normal position of the second and third molars.
  • Neither the ligation method nor the prescription adjustments placed in straight-wire brackets have anything to do with arch form, which is still established by the shape of the archwires.
  • Arch form is particularly important during the finishing stage of treatment, when heavy rectangular archwires are employed.
  • Wire-Bending Robots: In lingual orthodontics, the scanned casts needed for fabrication of custom bracket pads also provide the data needed to generate computer-fabricated archwires (Incognito). For labial orthodontics, SureSmile (OraMetrix, Richardson, TX) uses data acquired via a direct intraoral scan or CBCT to shape finishing archwires to the desired arch form and adjust it at each bracket to provide correct in–out, angulation, and torque bends. A randomized clinical trial would be needed to determine whether the use of computer-formed finishing wires really reduced treatment time for comparable outcomes.
  • Clear Polymer Archwires offer two potential advantages over stainless steel or titanium: better esthetics, and physical properties that may equal or exceed those of metal archwires. Problems with wire stability and discoloration diminished the enthusiasm to the point that further progress will be needed to make them an acceptable choice in clinical treatment.
  • Coated Archwires: Initially, these coatings were easily lost. More recently the coatings have become better, but their esthetic value still is at risk over time.
Temporary Anchorage Devices

I Bone Screws

  • Most screws now are formed from titanium to take advantage of its greater biocompatibility.
  • Bone screws can be used readily as either direct or indirect anchorage Fig 10.49.
  • The key characteristics of any TAD are: its short- and long-term stability (the major indicator of success or failure) and its ease of use (Box 10.2)
  • Stability:
    • Short-term or primary stability is determined by mechanical retention of the screw in bone, which depends on bone properties, the design of the screw, and placement technique.
    • Long-term or secondary stability is defined by the biologic union of the screw to the surrounding bone. It is determined by the implant surface, bone characteristics, and bone turnover.
    • Over time, primary stability decreases while secondary stability increases; clinical stability is the sum of primary and secondary stability and is the major factor in clinical success Fig 10.47.
  • Factors in stability-related success that have been shown to be important are:
    1. The pitch of the screw threads (how close the threads are to one another). The denser the bone, the closer the threads should be. Because the layer of cortical bone is thin in the dental alveolus, a tighter pitch of the threads near the head of the screw gives greater contact with the cortical bone, higher pull-out strength, and better primary stability.
    2. The length of the screw. The amount of contact with cortical bone is the major factor in stability, and the amount of soft tissue overlying the bone is an important consideration. (A long screw that passes all the way through the alveolus to reach cortical bone on the other side called a bicortical screw).
    3. The diameter of the screw. Within the 1.3- to 2.0-mm diameter range, stability and survival are much more strongly related to the amount of cortical bone contact rather than the screw diameter
    4. The form of the tip. All orthodontic miniscrews are self-tapping (i.e., they create their own thread as they advance). There are two self-tapping designs: thread-forming and thread-cutting.
      • A thread-forming screw compresses the bone around the thread as the screw advances, obtains better bone-to-screw contact, and is better adapted for use with alveolar bone.
      • A thread-cutting screw improve penetration into denser bone, they perform better in the mandibular ramus, mandibular buccal shelf, zygomatic buttress, and palate.
Reversed in 7th ed — exam-worthy Root proximity is now a MAJOR cause of screw failure. The 6th edition taught that root proximity was not a major factor (and that contacting the PDL did not cause ankylosis). The 7th edition reverses this: recent clinical and histological studies show root proximity is one of the major reasons for screw failure, an effect more obvious in the mandible — illustrated by a new success-rate-by-proximity figure Fig 10.46.
New in 7th ed — numbers For interradicular sites, diameters of 1.3 to 1.5 mm and a length of 5 to 7 mm are recommended. (The difference between the two self-tapping designs is the cutting flute on the tip of the thread-cutting screw.)
  • Ease of Use:
    • Whether a pilot hole is needed. Self-drilling screws do not need a pilot hole beyond the cortical plate and can penetrate the cortical plate if it is thin. If the cortical plate is difficult to penetrate, a pilot hole can decrease insertion torque and potential for screw fracture.
    • Whether a tissue punch is needed.
    • The ease or difficulty of turning the screw as it is inserted, while keeping pressure on it. Strong resistance to turning the screw at that point reflects high insertion torque. This increases primary stability, but it can lead to fracture of the screw, increased microdamage to the bone, and decreased secondary stability.
    • The design of the area of the head to which a wire, spring, or elastomeric will be attached.
  • Linked Screws in Palatal Anchorage. The palate is an excellent place for bone screws, with the greatest bone density found anteriorly and lateral to the midline. Screws in the palate almost always are used in pairs and often are linked together to stabilize a small plate that has attachments to reach the dentition Fig 10.50.

II Miniplates

  • The most frequent location for miniplates as anchorage for repositioning maxillary teeth vertically or sagittally is at the base of the zygomatic arch (but the linked screws in the palate are used even more often for the same purpose).
  • For repositioning multiple mandibular teeth, either bone screws or miniplates are most often placed on the buccal shelf of bone below the lower molars.
  • The major determinants of stability are:
    • The number of screws with which the plate is attached "three screws are preferred" Fig 10.53.
    • The age of the patient. Bone maturity does not reach the level for good retention of the screws before approximately age 11.
  • Comparing alveolar bone screws with miniplates Table 10.5.
New in 7th ed — comparison data The 7th edition adds quantitative comparison tables to guide the choice between alveolar screws, palatal screws, and miniplates — a miniplate failure-rate table Table 10.4 and a head-to-head bone screws vs miniplates table Table 10.5 (your summary's "Table 10.6").
